issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette:
Ethan was twenty-one, married less than a year, and working as a social ministry coordinator in a mid-sized city when his relief agency sent him on a six-week deployment to a conflict zone in the Middle East. Three weeks in, his convoy was ambushed near a contested village. Mortar rounds slammed into the dirt road ahead; men shouted in Arabic from behind a wrecked truck; a military vehicle roared past firing into the air. Ethan huddled in the back of a van, certain he was going to die. He survived physically unharmed, but the memory refused to stay in the past. Even after he returned home, the scene would crash into his mind with the same paralyzing terror he had felt that afternoon-his heart pounding, his skin cold, as if the dust and shouting were happening right here in his quiet apartment. Sometimes he sat up in bed and had to touch the carpet to convince himself he was no longer there. Because the memory felt so present and real, it sensitized Ethan to any sensory cue-a sudden noise, a certain pitch of voice-that could have belonged to the ambush, making those cues into triggers he could not ignore. The story felt unreal, too extreme to have actually happened to him, yet it did not feel like a memory. It felt like the present.

In the weeks that followed, Ethan began to notice how easily the past came alive. When his wife mentioned a news story about military operations, his stomach dropped and his thoughts were suddenly back in the convoy. The same thing happened if he heard Arabic being spoken on the street or in a grocery store-even a friendly conversation would make him freeze, his throat tight. Shouting in any language was worse. At work, where his ministry sometimes hosted refugee families, he began to avoid the common room during afternoon tea, knowing someone might bring up wartime experiences. Talking about the event itself, even with his wife, felt unthinkable; the moment the topic surfaced, his mind flooded with images and sounds and he lost the ability to speak.

The immediate effect of these triggers was a surge of threat. Ethan started scanning strangers who approached him-a man reaching for the same cereal box, a woman walking too quickly in his direction. Any sudden movement put him on guard, and he began waking during the night to check whether the door was locked and the apartment was safe, even though there was no danger. This constant sense of danger taught Ethan to scan his environment for anything that might confirm the threat, so that he began interpreting ordinary events-a person walking briskly, a car door slamming-as triggers that demanded his full attention. That feeling of danger, once activated, would throw him straight back into the memory: the smell of diesel, the shouting, the thud of the mortar. Each time his threat system fired, the memory felt more present, more impossible to shake.

To manage it all, Ethan developed habits that made sense to him at first. He stayed up very late, sometimes past two in the morning, because the moment he tried to sleep the flashes would come. He found himself replaying the ambush over and over, trying to work out what he could have done differently-if the convoy had taken another road, if they had left an hour earlier-as though finding the right prevention strategy might drain the memory of its power. And he began turning down invitations that might make him feel happy or hopeful: a meal with friends, a weekend trip with his wife, the prospect of a promotion at work. Joy felt dangerous, like a betrayal of the terror he still carried, and he was terrified that if he let himself hope, something terrible would happen again.

The rumination itself kept the memory sharp. Every night he spent dissecting the event strengthened its vividness and its unreality at the same time. The more he tried to prevent the past, the more it dominated his present. His wife grew worried. Ethan withdrew from her, too, not wanting to burden her with his fears. At church, he started arriving late and leaving early to avoid casual conversation. By the time he finally agreed to see a therapist, he was sleeping less than four hours a night, flinching at the sound of his own name, and dreading the moment someone would bring up a military topic or speak an Arabic word. What frightened him most was the feeling that the memory was still happening-that he had never really left that road. He came to therapy hoping to find a way back to the present, and to the life he had before the ambush.
